U.S. Tariffs on Imported Apparel Hit Retailers, Leading to Store Closures and Job Cuts

WASHINGTON, June 17—A new round of tariffs on imported apparel and footwear, imposed by the U.S. government last month, is sharply impacting domestic retail firms, with industry groups reporting widespread job cuts and store closures as companies scramble to adapt to rapidly rising costs.

The trade-policy measure, announced in early May, levies a 25% tariff on a wide range of clothing and footwear imported from several major supplier countries. The move, part of a broader effort to bolster American manufacturing, has left retailers facing higher prices at a time of already thin margins and cautious consumer spending.

According to the National Retail Merchants Federation, more than 1,100 retail outlets have closed or announced plans to close since the tariffs took effect. “Small and mid-sized retailers are being hit the hardest,” said federation president Karen Ramos. “They simply don’t have the scale or resources to absorb these cost increases or to renegotiate contracts on short notice.”

Workers in the sector have begun to feel the effects. Retailers across the country, from large chains to local stores, have reported layoffs in recent weeks. In the Midwest, ValueMart, a discount chain with 150 locations, announced it would cut 900 jobs and shutter 18 stores by the end of the quarter. In a statement, ValueMart CEO Donald Chen said, “We regret the impact on our employees and communities, but the tariff-related cost surge leaves us no choice.”

Industry analysts say the sudden imposition of tariffs has disrupted ordering cycles and forced firms to reevaluate their inventory strategies. “Retailers are caught in a bind. Many have shipments in transit that were ordered months ago, before the tariffs were announced, and now those goods are significantly more expensive,” said Alana Vega, retail analyst at MarketSight Research. “Some stores are raising prices, but others fear losing customers if they do.”

Unions representing retail workers have called on the government to reconsider the policy. “Our members are facing layoffs and reduced hours, and the uncertainty is taking a toll,” said Mike Latham, spokesperson for the National Retail Employees Union.

The U.S. Trade Office stated this week that the tariffs will remain in place pending further review, emphasizing the administration’s commitment to “leveling the playing field for American businesses.” Meanwhile, retailers continue to assess the impact on their operations, with many bracing for further disruption as the busy back-to-school shopping season approaches.
